opus-5.5.text:
I think solving math problems is really just the most visible tip of the iceberg. When people hear "AI for math," they picture a system that takes a competition problem and spits out an answer. That's a great benchmark, and it's been an important way to measure progress, but it's not where I think the deepest value lies.

The first thing I'd point to is that mathematics is the language of rigorous reasoning. If you can build a system that genuinely reasons mathematically, especially one that works in a formal setting, where every step can be mechanically verified, you're building something that can't fool itself. That matters enormously, because one of the core problems with today's AI systems is that they can sound very confident while being wrong. Math, particularly formal math with proof assistants like Lean, gives you a ground truth. The proof either checks or it doesn't. So I see AI for math as a kind of training ground for trustworthy reasoning in general.

The second piece is verification beyond mathematics itself. Huge parts of our world run on things that are, at bottom, mathematical objects: software, hardware designs, cryptographic protocols, financial systems, control systems for aircraft. Today, formally verifying that a chip or a piece of critical code does what it's supposed to do is incredibly expensive and requires rare human expertise. If AI can make formal verification cheap and scalable, that changes how we build safe software and safe systems, and as AI writes more and more of our code, being able to verify that code becomes even more urgent.

Third, there's the question of what this does for mathematicians and scientists. I don't think the right picture is AI replacing mathematicians. It's closer to giving every mathematician a tireless collaborator who can check the tedious lemmas, search across the literature, try a hundred variations of an approach overnight, and formalize an argument so the community can trust it. That could change the sociology of math. Big proofs today sometimes take years for the community to verify. Collaboration could scale in ways that are hard to imagine right now, with large teams of humans and AI working on different pieces of a program and everything stitched together formally.

And then, more speculatively but I think quite importantly, math sits upstream of a lot of science. Physics, theoretical computer science, economics, and parts of biology all rely on mathematical structure. A system that can discover new mathematical concepts, not just prove statements someone else wrote down, could open new ways of thinking in those fields too.

So for me, the broader potential is this: math is the cleanest environment we have for building AI that reasons reliably, and once you have that, the applications go far beyond the olympiad problem on the screen. It's really about building a foundation of verifiable intelligence.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the framing of "AI for Math" as solving competition problems or benchmark problems actually undersells what's happening, and I'd push back on it a little.

The way I see it, mathematics is really the foundational language of reasoning. If you can build systems that reason rigorously in mathematics, where every step has to be verifiable and there's no room for hand-waving, you've built something that generalizes far beyond math itself. Formal verification is a great example. The same machinery that proves a theorem in Lean can prove that a piece of software, or a cryptographic protocol, or a control system in an aircraft, behaves exactly as specified. Right now that kind of verification is enormously expensive because it requires highly trained humans writing proofs line by line. If AI can do that work, you suddenly get a world where critical infrastructure can be provably correct rather than just well-tested.

The second thing is that math is a bottleneck for a lot of science. Physics, economics, biology, machine learning itself, they all hit walls that are fundamentally mathematical. A physicist might have the right intuition for a model but lack the tools to analyze it. Historically you needed the right mathematician to happen to be interested in your problem. If mathematical capability becomes something you can call on demand, the pace of discovery in those adjacent fields changes dramatically.

And then there's something more philosophical, which is the question of what mathematics itself becomes. Today we have maybe a few tens of thousands of research mathematicians in the world, and the subject has fragmented so much that two experts in different subfields can barely read each other's papers. AI could act as a translator and a connector, finding that a technique in algebraic geometry is secretly the same as something in combinatorics. That kind of synthesis has historically produced the biggest leaps, and it's exactly what humans are worst at because no single person can hold all of it in their head.

So when I think about the broader potential, I think about trustworthiness, acceleration of science, and a change in the structure of knowledge itself. Solving problems is the entry point, but it's really not the destination.

astra-6.text:
I think solving problems is one part of it, but the broader opportunity is to help us discover new mathematics. A lot of mathematical research happens before you have a clearly stated problem: you’re looking at examples, noticing patterns, deciding what the right definition is, and asking which questions are worth pursuing.

AI could help throughout that process. It could explore examples with us, suggest conjectures, or identify connections between areas that use very different language. And if we can pair that exploration with reliable proof verification, we could have a powerful feedback loop between intuition and rigor.

For me, the exciting possibility is that AI changes who can participate in mathematics and what they can explore. A student could have a patient partner to help them build intuition, while a researcher could investigate ideas that would otherwise take too much time to pursue. The ambition is broader than getting answers faster—it’s expanding our capacity to ask interesting questions and understand the answers.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could help discover mathematics by exploring examples and suggesting conjectures.

r002.rationale: It mentions proof verification creating a feedback loop, but does not state that a proving AI provides a reward signal to a conjecturing AI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think solving problems is only one part of doing mathematics. There’s also deciding which questions are worth asking, forming conjectures, finding useful definitions, and building connections between areas that initially look unrelated. AI could potentially help with that whole process.

For example, a system might explore examples with you, notice a pattern, and suggest a conjecture. Then you could work together to understand why it’s true—or find a counterexample that points toward a better question. That would make AI a partner in mathematical discovery, beyond producing answers to questions we already know how to formulate.

There’s also an educational opportunity: helping more people develop mathematical intuition and access ideas that would otherwise require a lot of specialized background. To me, the broader potential is expanding both what mathematics we can discover and who gets to participate in discovering it.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could notice patterns and suggest mathematical conjectures, as part of discovery beyond producing answers.

r002.rationale: It describes working to understand a conjecture or find a counterexample, but does not say that a proving AI can provide a reward signal to a conjecturing AI.
